item.title: Strawberry launches fundraising for its new playground
item.description: The Strawberry Recreation District has begun asking residents to help pay for its new playground under a program that would run from a $1,500 tile in aThe Strawberry Recreation District has begun asking residents to help pay for its new playground under a program that would run from a $1,500 tile in a mosaic to naming rights over the playground itself. mosaic to naming rights over the playground itself.
item.content:encoded:
The Strawberry Recreation District has begun asking residents to help pay for its new playground under a recognition schedule that would run from a $1,500 tile in a mosaic to naming rights over the playground itself.

The board approved a $2.4 million contract in July with playground company GameTime for a 12,799-square-foot play area off Belvedere Drive, centered on a climbable 20-foot-tall berry with two green slides for arms and bouncy footbridges. The district plans to break ground in 2027.

As drafted, donors who give less than $1,500 would be recognized on the district’s website. Above that the schedule offers permanent inscriptions on a bench, a picnic table, the park entry sign or a mosaic a local artist would make, rising to exclusive naming rights over the turf soccer field at $250,000 and over the playground at $500,000. Three levels are capped: 100 mosaic tiles, 10 benches and 10 picnic tables.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister

item.title: ‘Living shoreline’ restoration at Blackie’s starts after Labor Day
item.description: Work to rebuild two eroding beaches at Blackie's Pasture in Tiburon begins the day after Labor Day, using sand, gravel and logs instead of seawalls and riprap.
item.content:encoded:
Work to rebuild two eroding beaches at Blackie’s Pasture is set to begin the day after Labor Day, using sand, gravel and logs instead of seawalls and riprap to hold the shoreline in place.

The Tiburon Town Council voted 3-0 Aug. 19 to award the construction contract to Livermore-based Goodfellow Bros. for $468,983 and to let the town manager approve change orders of up to 15%, or $70,347, bringing the maximum to $539,330.

Goodfellow will grade back the eroding scarp, the steep face where the beach has been cut away. Crews will also remove and dispose of asphalt, install two rock sills at Brunini Beach and place a log backstop at Greenwood Beach.

“We’re installing a living shoreline, meaning that the material that’s being installed here at this beach, the wave action will pull the material out and push it back in so that it doesn’t erode any of the areas along Blackie’s Pasture,” said David Eshoo, the town Public Works Department’s engineering manager.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: A project drawing shows the two beaches at Blackie’s Pasture as they would be rebuilt, with the beachface and backshore beach in tan, cobble-armored salt marsh and drift sills in green and the edges where vegetation is expected to take hold. The Tiburon Town Council awarded a $468,983 construction contract Aug. 19 to rebuild about 1.4 acres of shoreline along Greenwood and Brunini beaches with sand, gravel and logs instead of seawalls and riprap, and work is set to begin Sept. 8. (via town of Tiburon)

item.title: Tiburon will clear Railroad Marsh ahead of strong El Niño
item.description: Tiburon will strip about 1,800 tons of cattail, invasive plants and sediment from Railroad Marsh this fall to restore the basin's capacity to hold storm runoff.
item.content:encoded:
Crews will strip about 1,800 tons of cattail, invasive plants and sediment from Railroad Marsh this fall, restoring the basin’s capacity to hold storm runoff ahead of a winter federal forecasters put at better than a 90% chance of a very strong El Niño.

The Tiburon Town Council voted 4-0 Aug. 19 to hire Lafayette-based McNabb Construction Inc. for the work at a cost not to exceed $274,743 and to let the town manager approve change orders of up to 10%, bringing the ceiling to $302,217. Vice Mayor Isaac Nikfar was absent.

The contract sends the firm back to the marsh, where it did the town’s maintenance work last fall. McNabb was not the low bidder. Petaluma-based Land Revision bid $264,600, about $10,000 less, and Dixon Marine Services bid $386,237.

Public Works Engineering Manager David Eshoo told the council that staff will try to negotiate McNabb down to Land Revision’s price and that he does not expect to spend the contingency.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: Cattail and other vegetation crowd the water’s edge on Sept. 24, 2025, at Railroad Marsh in Tiburon, with the Point Tiburon Marsh condominiums in the background. The Town Council on Aug. 19 authorized a contract to strip about 1,800 tons of cattail, invasive plants and sediment from the basin this fall, restoring its capacity to hold storm runoff ahead of a winter forecasters expect to bring a strong El Niño (Kevin Hessel archive / The Ark 2025).

item.title: Tiburon monthly financial reports begin as audits lag
item.description: Tiburon's Town Council got its first monthly financial report Aug. 19, following months of resident pressure for more transparency about the town's books.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon’s Town Council received its first monthly financial report Aug. 19, a package that summed up the fiscal year that ended June 30, tallied the town’s cash and investments through July and laid out a decade of revenue and spending. Town Manager Greg Chanis cautioned that the year-end numbers are preliminary.

The presentation followed months of pressure from residents for more financial transparency, including calls to speed up the town’s audits and to create an independent finance committee like Belvedere’s.

Earlier in the meeting, on a separate item, Chanis addressed a question that has run through the criticism. Letters to the council had flagged revenue from hotel taxes, known as the transient occupancy tax, as coming in light for the year — the reports show the town’s two hotels generating $604,458 against $875,000 budgeted, a gap of $270,542. Chanis said that gap is an artifact of timing, not a shortfall. The tax arrives quarterly, in large chunks, and the final quarter ran six weeks late.

“Long story short, it looks like we’re going to exceed the budgeted revenue by several thousand dollars in (transient occupancy taxes),” Chanis said. “So the concern about a dramatic drop in (the tax) is not reality.”
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez

item.title: New principal brings public-school experience to St. Hilary
item.description: Waylon Miller, the new principal of St. Hilary School in Tiburon, ran a public high school in Hayward. He says he wanted a job that let him bring his faith to work.
item.content:encoded:
Waylon Miller has taught second grade, coached wrestling and run a public high school. What he wanted next, the new principal of St. Hilary School says, was a job that let him bring his faith to work.

“I wanted to work in an environment where I could blend both my faith and my career into one opportunity,” Miller says. “And work with students to continue to get the most out of them and show them pathways towards better learning and better life.”

Miller, 46, who lives in Fremont, has taken over as principal of the Catholic school on Hilary Drive in Tiburon, where classes started Aug. 24. He replaces Marie Bordeleau, who left at the end of September 2025 after 11 years in the job.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister

item.title: Author draws on Tiburon Peninsula roots for her first children’s book
item.description: Christina Altick grew up in Belvedere and Tiburon. Her first children's book, "Whimsy, the Little Dachshund," draws on the safety and warmth she remembers from the peninsula.
item.content:encoded:
Christina Altick says growing up on the Tiburon Peninsula felt like something out of a storybook.

She recalls spending time outdoors walking the family dog, a golden retriever named Eva; spending summers at Lake Tahoe; and taking trips to Michigan to visit her grandparents.

“I have such amazing memories,” says Altick, adding that the peninsula was “such an amazing place to grow up, so safe.”

Altick’s first children’s book, “Whimsy, the Little Dachshund: A Cozy Cottage Tale,” aims to capture that feeling for a generation of young readers. She self-published the book in June through Spines, an online publishing platform.

Inspired by her English cream miniature dachshund, Lachlan Skye, the illustrated story follows a gentle dachshund through the changing seasons in an English village, inviting children and adults to slow down and notice the small, comforting details of everyday life.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: Christina Altick holds a copy of her children’s book ‘Whimsy, the Little Dachshund’ on July 11 during a signing at Emily Joubert Home & Garden in Larkspur’s Marin Country Mart. Altick, who grew up in Belvedere and Tiburon and now lives in San Francisco, self-published the book in June. (via Christina Altick)

item.title: Everyday Encounters: A former medical sales rep enjoys retirement with husband and dog
item.description: Now retired from a long career in medical-device sales, Tiburon’s Bonnie Bates has a new boss these days: her dog, Harper.
item.content:encoded:
Now retired from a long career in medical-device sales, Tiburon’s Bonnie Bates has a new boss these days: her dog, Harper.

Walking Harper at Shoreline Park on Aug. 19, Bates says the dog, about a year and a half old, loves to walk and run and has brought some structure to retirement.

“She’s kind of my new job,” Bates says.

For Bates, retirement has been less about slowing down and more about shifting gears. She walks Harper every day, bikes around Marin and still seeks out the kind of adventure that has shaped much of her life, from growing up in the Colorado mountains to traveling through Europe with her husband.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: Tiburon resident Bonnie Bates sits with her dog, Harper, on Aug. 19 at Shoreline Park in Tiburon. Bates, who retired from a career in medical-device sales, says the golden retriever, about a year and a half old, has brought structure to her retirement. (Tyler Callister / The Ark)

item.title: Richard ‘Dick’ DeNezza
item.description: Richard “Dick” DeNezza passed away on August 13th at 88 years young.
item.content:encoded:
Richard “Dick” DeNezza passed away on August 13th at 88 years young. He joins his late wife, Patricia DeNezza, after being apart for nearly 25 years.

He was born in 1938 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, to Rose and Eugene. He graduated from Central Catholic High School, then attended University of Pittsburgh where he earned his bachelor’s in electrical engineering and his MBA.

He served in the Air Force as a captain and later joined the National Security Agency and Control Data Corporation. Dick had various careers working as a real-estate developer and other entrepreneurial ventures. Pat often said as soon as he made all the mistakes in one business, it was time to start a new one. His job often took him internationally, where he worked in Germany, Russia, Japan, China and Hungary.

Dick moved to Tiburon in 1978 where he and Pat raised their family. He served as a member and president of the Rotary Club of Tiburon-Belvedere, and was a devout member of St. Mary’s Star of the Sea Parish and served as the president of their Men’s Club.

Dick will be remembered for his optimism, charitable heart, faith, and love of family. He is remembered by his three children: Christine, Matt, and Tim, and 11 grandchildren. He will be missed every day. In his memory, consider making a donation to St. Jude’s or Tunnel to Towers.

Join us at St. Mary’s Star of the Sea for a Vigil September 13 at 6pm and Mass September 14 at 10am with reception to follow.
item.dc:creator: Reader submitted

item.title: SF State's Estuary & Ocean Science Center in Tiburon will close after fight to save it falls short
item.description: San Francisco State will close its Romberg Tiburon Campus on Sept. 30, ending a four-year fight to save the only marine research center on San Francisco Bay's shores.
item.content:encoded:
With fall approaching, it’s almost time for Discovery Day, a day of hands-on marine science for Bay Area children at the Estuary & Ocean Science Center. But not this year. This year, the halls will be dark, the seawater tanks will be empty, the scientists gone and the gates to the Romberg Tiburon Campus padlocked indefinitely.

Despite desperate attempts to save it, San Francisco State University’s marine-biology field station will close Sept. 30, according to interim Executive Director Katharyn Boyer and university administrators.

Boyer’s announcement ends a four-year struggle to save the 53-acre facility in unincorporated Tiburon after the university said it could no longer afford to maintain it “with continued declines in enrollment, and a budget that won’t balance,” she wrote in an Aug. 11 letter.

“At the same time, deferred maintenance, inherited in 1978 at the time of the property’s transfer, has become much worse over time,” she wrote. “We have known for years that the … campus would need to become self-supporting; however, maintenance and operation funds have been very difficult to find.”
item.dc:creator: Gretchen Lang
item.media:description: San Francisco State will close its Romberg Tiburon Campus on Sept. 30, ending a four-year fight to save the only marine research center on San Francisco Bay's shores.

item.title: Caltrans to begin Tiburon Boulevard work by September
item.description: Caltrans expects to start its 4.6-mile Tiburon Boulevard maintenance project by the end of August or in September, with repaving targeted for next spring.
item.content:encoded:
Caltrans expects to begin work on its 4.6-mile preventive maintenance project along Tiburon Boulevard by the end of August or in September, with the repaving of the road targeted for next spring.

Agency spokesperson Matt O’Donnell told The Ark last week construction is expected to last until July 2027, as Caltrans plans to pause work during the winter months.

The project runs from just outside Mill Valley limits to downtown Tiburon along state-owned Highway 131, which doubles as East Blithedale Avenue in Mill Valley and as Tiburon Boulevard east of the southbound Highway 101 on-ramp. Work will begin at East Blithedale’s intersection with Tower Drive and end at the downtown Tiburon roundabout near Main Street, where Tiburon Boulevard becomes Paradise Drive, O’Donnell said.

Weekly construction-planning meetings are taking place this month, O’Donnell said, and more specific information on traffic advisories will be released in the coming weeks.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez

item.title: Residents weigh updates to Tiburon ponds site park design
item.description: Residents pressed for more stone seating and questioned whether new plantings would block water views as a Tiburon parks subcommittee showed an updated design for the ponds site.
item.content:encoded:
Residents pressed for more stone seating along the hillside and questioned whether new plantings would block water views as a Tiburon parks subcommittee presented an updated design for the former sanitation ponds site near McKegney Green.

How to fund construction also came up. David Eshoo, the town’s public works engineering manager and the subcommittee’s staff liaison, gave the group a rough estimate of more than $3 million. Tiburon residents’ earliest opportunity to approve a tax or bond for it will not come until the November 2028 election.

The subcommittee met Aug. 13 in the Community Room at Tiburon Town Hall, three days after Mill Valley-based RHAA Landscape Architecture & Planning submitted its 60%-complete design, said Parks, Open Space & Trails Commission Chair Michael Moon, who sits on the ponds subcommittee with Commissioner Nicole Voss.

Last week’s informal session will not be residents’ last chance to comment. A special parks commission meeting Aug. 24 will include discussion of the design, followed by the commission’s regular meeting Sept. 15 and a public workshop that has not been scheduled, Eshoo said in an email last week.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: Parks, Open Space & Trails Commission Chair Michael Moon presents the 60%-complete design for the former sanitation ponds site near McKegney Green during a workshop Aug. 13 at Tiburon Town Hall. Moon and Commissioner Nicole Voss make up the subcommittee guiding the project, which goes back to the full commission at a special meeting Aug. 24. (Francisco Martinez / The Ark)

item.title: Tiburon neighbors rally to find lost dog, bring him home
item.description: Apollo, a French bulldog-pug mix, broke his leash. A drone with thermal detection, a PawBoost listing and local volunteers all joined the two-day search.
item.content:encoded:
Apollo, a French bulldog-pug mix, was on a leash outside Mary Jasek’s Old Tiburon home Aug. 4, basking in the sun while she cleaned inside, when something spooked him. He bolted, Jasek says, “with such great force that he broke away from the leash.”

Jasek, who was dog-sitting for her daughter and son-in-law, ran through Old Tiburon’s hilly streets, searching and calling for him. She posted on Nextdoor, asking neighbors to watch for the dog.

The community responded almost immediately, she says.

“I had three people just show up in their car, look at me and roll their windows down and just say, … ‘Are you Mary?’” Jasek recalls. “And they said they were looking.”

Businesses put up lost-dog flyers, mail carriers watched for him and Tiburon Peninsula residents joined the search, in person and by sharing Jasek’s post online.

One of Jasek’s neighbors found Apollo two days later, Aug. 6, in Old St. Hilary’s Open Space Preserve and reunited him with Jasek, her daughter Dana Jasek and son-in-law Zachary D’Agostino of Marinwood.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: Marinwood residents Dana Jasek and Zachary D’Agostino and Tiburon resident Mary Jasek, Dana’s mom, reunited with Apollo Aug. 6 following two days of searching after the dog broke from his leash and ran away while Mary Jasek was dog-sitting. (Francisco Martinez / The Ark)

item.title: Belvedere drops Mallard Pointe project manager
item.description: Belvedere has cut ties with the consulting firm it hired in April to oversee the Mallard Pointe redevelopment, weeks before demolition could begin on the 22-unit complex.
item.content:encoded:
Belvedere has cut ties with the consulting firm it hired four months ago to oversee the Mallard Pointe redevelopment, leaving the city without a third-party project manager weeks before demolition could begin on the 22-unit lagoon-side complex.

The city contracted with Phillips Seabrook Associates of Santa Rosa on April 13 to oversee the 40-unit development on Belvedere Lagoon. The position was not optional: The conditions of approval the council attached to Mallard Pointe commit the city to retaining a part-time consultant to handle day-to-day coordination among the developer, city staff and residents, something residents had pressed the city for. Councilmembers discussed what they wanted from the role at their February retreat, and that feedback shaped the request for proposals. Three firms responded and all three were interviewed.

In an Aug. 10 newsletter, the city said it had decided to end its engagement with the firm.

Planning and Building Director Rebecca Markwick, answering questions by email, said the city reassessed its needs for the role and went looking for other firms with “a different mix of skills and expertise.” She said Aug. 14 that Belvedere was interviewing firms and expected to select a replacement within two weeks.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister

item.title: New fitness studio approved for downtown Tiburon
item.description: Five Points Fitness plans free weights, cardio, self-adjusting strength machines and a recovery area with two kinds of saunas. The owners are targeting a February 2027 opening.
item.content:encoded:
A membership gym offering free weights, cardio equipment, self-adjusting strength machines and saunas is coming to a downtown Tiburon storefront that has sat empty since 2022.

The Tiburon Planning Commission on Aug. 12 granted Five Points Fitness a conditional-use permit to open an 8,090-square-foot gym across two floors at 1620 Tiburon Blvd. Recreation and entertainment uses are allowed in the property’s mixed-use zone only with a use permit, and the space had most recently been offices. The vote was 3-0, with Chair Daniel Amir and Vice Chair Eric Woodward absent. No one spoke during public comment.

Tom MacDonald, who co-owns the gym with Bryan LeFebure, said after the meeting that they’re targeting a February 2027 opening, pending construction permits and schedules.

The Tiburon location would be the company’s third. MacDonald told the commission that he and LeFebure bought the Corte Madera gym from World Gym about 21 years ago and have run the Novato gym for 11 years.

item.title: Tiburon Fire rejects grand jury timeline for consolidation talks
item.description: The Tiburon Fire Protection District board votedto partially disagree with all seven Marin County civil grand jury findings and to decline five of its nine recommendations.
item.content:encoded:
The Tiburon Fire Protection District board has told the Marin County civil grand jury it will not meet the jury’s deadlines for exploring consolidation with neighboring agencies, saying it will pursue shared services on its own schedule.

The board approved the district’s formal response 4-0 at its Aug. 12 meeting, with several minor additions and with board member Rick Jones absent. The response partially disagrees with all seven findings in the jury’s report, “Better Service at Lower Cost: Optimizing Essential Services for the Future of Marin,” and says the district will not implement five of the nine recommendations, which it called not warranted or not reasonable.

The report, released June 11, urged Marin’s more than 50 special districts — including fire, water, sanitation and refuse agencies — to accelerate consolidation talks, expand shared administrative services and publish standardized performance metrics. It said the county’s fragmented system duplicates administrative work, produces uneven costs and service levels and leaves some districts without the scale for long-term investment.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister

item.title: Report: Open creek sent skiers toward fatal avalanche path
item.description: Guides who led a Tiburon mother of three into a fatal Sierra avalanche were steering away from the slide path when an open creek turned them back, a commissioned report says.
item.content:encoded:
Guides who led a Tiburon mother of three into a fatal Sierra avalanche were steering the group away from the slide path when an open creek turned them back, according to a report their company commissioned.

The report does not say why the guides pressed on toward the trailhead after the crossing failed instead of returning to the huts they had left two hours earlier. Blackbird Mountain Guides, the Truckee company that ran the trip, has not addressed the question publicly.

Kate Morse, a 45-year-old biotech executive whose two eldest daughters compete for Sugar Bowl Academy, was one of six women killed in the Feb. 17 slide. They were part of a group of eight friends whose children ski for the academy near Donner Summit. Three guides died with them.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Hessel

item.title: Mildred Frances Minter (Milly) Jewell
item.description: Former Tiburon resident Mildred Frances Minter (Milly) Jewell, age 102, died July 3, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Former Tiburon resident Mildred Frances Minter (Milly) Jewell, age 102, died peacefully with her daughters at her side on July 3, 2026, at her home in The Tamalpais/Sequoia Living senior residence in Greenbrae, California.

Milly Jewell was born on April 25, 1924, in Cedar County, Missouri, to Virgil Artemis Minter and Ada Byrd Minter (née Reid). She earned her bachelor’s degree in journalism from the University of Missouri at Columbia, then moved to Chicago to work in communications for the National Safety Council. In Chicago, she met her future husband, Albert Hartwell Jewell Jr., then a medical student at Northwestern. They married in 1952 during Dr. Jewell’s surgery residency in Ann Arbor, Michigan, and moved to Marin County, California, in 1959.

Milly was a homemaker and active local volunteer. In the early 1970s, she spearheaded a drive to get a produce truck to come to her neighborhood so neighbors could buy produce directly from the farmers — a precursor to CSA farm boxes. With her keen interest in good food and trying new recipes, she cooked her way through Julia Child’s “Mastering the Art of French Cooking.” She volunteered in the Reed schools, her daughters’ Girl Scout troops, the Marin Art & Garden Center, the Marin County Free Library, the Tiburon Landmarks Society, and the Culinary Carnival, an annual event to raise money for Children’s Garden. She was also a longtime supporter of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco and the Achenbach Foundation for Graphic Arts.

With her husband, Milly made numerous opera-focused trips to Europe and travelled as well in Asia and Australia. In her later years, she hiked in the Sierras and abroad, and frequently walked the Tiburon bike path with her Belvedere and Tiburon friends, who informally called their group “The Fallen Arches.” After she and her husband moved to The Tamalpais in 1997, she became an avid player of bridge, Chinese-style Mahjongg, and gin rummy. Throughout her life, Milly was a voracious reader, often reading three books a week. The last book she finished, in the weeks before her death, was the just-published novel “Whistler” by Ann Patchett. She especially enjoyed poetry, writing some of her own and memorizing the poetry of others. She often had the perfect impromptu quote from Shakespeare, Alexander Pope, or Rilke (and, at parties, Ogden Nash or a limerick or two). Above all, she was devoted to each of her three grandsons, with whom she enjoyed close individual re...
item.dc:creator: Reader submitted

item.title: Janet Anne Benson (“Jan”) Pickett
item.description: Janet Anne Benson (“Jan”) Pickett, a Tiburon resident for over 40 years, passed away peacefully at her home on June 23, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Janet Anne Benson (“Jan”) Pickett, a Tiburon resident for over 40 years, passed away peacefully at her home on June 23, 2026, surrounded by her family after a courageous and lengthy battle with lung disease. Jan lived a beautiful, loving, and extraordinary life, and will be deeply missed by everyone who knew her.

Jan was born in Chicago on March 20, 1951, to John William and Mary Halpin Benson. She graduated from the University of Illinois with a B.A. degree, and she obtained master’s degrees from Southern Connecticut University in education and from the University of San Francisco in psychology. Jan was a teacher, a marriage and child counselor, and served as president of the Reed Union School District. Jan met her future husband Donn in grammar school (assuredly neither of them had the foggiest notion of any future together). They married right after their college graduations in 1973, and that special union endured for 53 years.

Jan’s true passion was being a mother and grandmother. She was a beloved and enduring matriarch — selfless, patient, caring, kind, wise, and unwaveringly positive. She will be remembered lovingly by her family and friends for so many of her unique contributions to their lives — her unceasing dedication and support of her ‘ohana. She had a special relationship to Hawaii and its aloha spirit.

Jan was renowned for her gift of throwing unforgettable and unique parties, her baking, particularly Christmas cookies (and as a teenager she won the first prize in a Northern Illinois cherry pie contest!); her hiking the hills above her home in Tiburon, especially to enjoy the poppies and other wildflowers; her Swedish Christmas celebrations to honor her heritage; her passion for playing charades and dice games; her loyalty to the Giants through thick and thin; her love of British police dramas; her special ability to grow beautiful gardens, particularly roses and dahlias; her sunrise walks along Lanikai Beach; her special Cosmo recipe; and her love of fireworks and Tahoe — best in combination. Jan also loved to travel and explore the world. She and Donn visited more than 65 countries while traveling to every continent, and (a particular Jan favorite) they took part in over 100 safari game drives during six trips to Africa.

Jan is survived by her husband, Donn; her daughter, Jessica (Parker) Lyons; her son, William (Emma) Pickett; four grandchildren, Johanna and Lillian Pickett, and Rose and Harvey Lyons; and he...

item.title: Garden Plot: Dragonflies bring beauty and benefits to local gardens
item.description: Dragonflies are carnivores that eat aphids, gnats, mosquitoes and flies, which makes them worth having around.
item.content:encoded:
Are you lucky enough to have dragonflies in your garden, or maybe have you seen them near fresh water such as the marsh behind the Belvedere-Tiburon Library? They are stunningly beautiful. I have a seasonal stream that seems to trickle all summer these days, so they’re around my garden, sometimes flying close to observe what I’m up to out there. There are some large dragonflies that are bright red, smaller ones that are a brilliant blue and some that are grayish. All are so much fun to watch.

Like bees and other insects, dragonflies have what appear to be huge eyes, which are actually compound eyes consisting of thousands of simple eyes. Fortunately, they’re harmless to us and don’t sting. Damselflies are the smaller ones; they have wings that fold into the shape of a V or over their backs when they are resting. Larger ones, called darners, have wings at right angles to their sides, and some can approach the size of a hummingbird.
item.dc:creator: Diane Lynch
item.media:description: This dragonfly, called a darner, is characterized by wings that are perpendicular to the body. The stream in my garden, shown here in winter, has a catch basin at the bottom where the dragonflies hang out in summer. (Diane Lynch / For The Ark)
